awake.gloss: To stop sleeping, or to rouse someone from sleep — a more literary word than *wake up* — and, figuratively, to stir something that was dormant.

senses.head: Stop sleeping
senses.body: Intransitive and a little literary; everyday American speech says *wake up*. Keep it apart from the adjective *awake* — *I was awake at four* is a state, not a past tense.
examples: I *awake* before the alarm most mornings.
She *awoke* to the sound of rain on the roof.
The whole house *had awoken* by six.

senses.head: Wake someone up
senses.body: Transitive, and rarer than the intransitive sense; most American writers reach for *wake* or the regular *awaken* here.
examples: Try not to *awake* the children when you come in.
The sirens *awoke* half the neighborhood.
The dog *has awoken* me at dawn every day this week.

senses.head: Stir up a feeling or memory
senses.body: Figurative and transitive, common in writing: a sight, a smell, or a story brings something dormant back to life.
examples: Something in the story *awoke* an old memory.
Small kindnesses *awake* loyalty in people.
The photographs *have awoken* a homesickness she thought was gone.

senses.head: awake to — become aware of
senses.body: Followed by a noun: to finally see something you had been ignoring. The adjective version, *be awake to*, is at least as common.
examples: The country slowly *awoke* to the scale of the problem.
We *awake* to our mistakes only after the fact.
Investors *have awoken* to the risk.

bear.gloss: To carry or support something, to endure it, or to bring it forth — plus the passive *be born*, the one sense that takes *born* instead of *borne*.

senses.head: Endure, put up with
senses.body: Very often negative or with *can't*: *I can't bear it*. The participle is *borne*, never *born*.
examples: I can't *bear* the sound of a dentist's drill.
She *bore* the delay without a word of complaint.
He *has borne* worse news than this.

senses.head: be born (passive only)
senses.body: Passive only, and the only sense spelled *born*. There is no active ✗ *she borned*; birth in the active takes *bear/bore/borne*.
examples: Their twins were *born* in a snowstorm.
He was *born* the year the mill closed.
All three of her children *had been born* by the time she turned thirty.

senses.head: Give birth to, bring forth
senses.body: The active birth sense, formal or literary; ordinary speech says *have a baby*. Here the participle is *borne*: *She has borne three children*.
examples: Mares usually *bear* one foal at a time.
She *bore* three children in five years.
The queen *had borne* no heir.

senses.head: Carry the weight of, support
senses.body: The structural sense — of beams, walls, ice, or a person carrying a burden or a cost.
examples: These beams *bear* the weight of the whole roof.
The ice *bore* his weight for two steps and then cracked.
The company *has borne* the legal fees since March.

senses.head: Carry, bring (formal)
senses.body: Formal or literary for physically carrying something from one place to another — *bearing gifts*, *bearing a message*.
examples: The servers *bear* trays over their heads.
The messengers *bore* the news from the capital.
Pilgrims *have borne* these relics along the same road for centuries.

senses.head: Produce, yield
senses.body: Of trees, investments, and efforts. *Bear fruit* works literally and figuratively; *bear interest* is the banking use.
examples: The old apple tree *bears* less fruit every year.
The account *bore* four percent interest.
Two years of talks *have borne* fruit at last.

senses.head: Have or show (a name, mark, resemblance)
senses.body: Of documents, buildings, and faces: to carry a name, a signature, a scar, or a likeness.
examples: The building *bears* her grandfather's name.
The check *bore* no signature.
The town *has borne* that name since 1802.

senses.head: bear in mind
senses.body: A fixed phrase, most often imperative, meaning to keep a fact in view while deciding something.
examples: *Bear* in mind that the office closes at four.
We *bore* in mind that she was new.
The committee *has borne* the deadline in mind throughout.

senses.head: bear with (someone)
senses.body: A request for patience, usually imperative: *bear with me*.
examples: *Bear* with me — this will take a minute.
She *bore* with his questions for a full hour.
Readers *have borne* with this digression long enough.

senses.head: Turn, veer in a direction
senses.body: Of a road, a vehicle, or a walker; also nautical. *Bear left*, *bear right*, *bear north*.
examples: *Bear* left where the road forks.
The trail *bore* east along the ridge.
We *had borne* too far south and lost the river.

senses.head: bear out — confirm
senses.body: Of evidence, data, or events proving a claim or a person right.
examples: The data *bear* out her theory.
The audit *bore* out every complaint.
Events *have borne* him out.

bespeak.gloss: A formal, literary verb meaning to be evidence of something; its past form *bespoke* leads a second life as a British adjective for custom-made goods.

senses.head: Be a sign of, give evidence of
senses.body: The only living verb sense in American English, and formal even then. The subject is almost always a thing — a voice, a room, a detail — not a person.
examples: Cracked paint and a sagging porch *bespeak* neglect.
The empty shelves *bespoke* a store about to close.
The silence *had bespoken* trouble long before anyone admitted it.
Her steady voice *bespeaks* years of practice.

senses.head: Order or arrange in advance
senses.body: Archaic: to speak for something ahead of time — a suit, a room, a dinner. This is the sense that produced the tailoring adjective.
examples: He *bespoke* a suit from a tailor on Savile Row.
In older novels a traveler would *bespeak* dinner at the inn.
The rooms *had been bespoken* months before the wedding.

senses.head: bespoke — custom-made (adjective)
senses.body: British, and not a verb use at all, though it is where most readers meet the form. Americans say *custom-made*, *made-to-order*, or *custom*.
examples: He wears a *bespoke* suit to every hearing.
The firm sells *bespoke* software to hospitals.

bite.gloss: To cut or grip something with the teeth — and, by extension, to sting, to grip a surface, or to take hold painfully.

senses.head: Cut or grip with the teeth
senses.body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. Remember the split: past *bit*, participle *bitten* — ✗ *I have bit my tongue*.
examples: Dogs *bite* when they are frightened.
The neighbor's terrier *bit* the mail carrier last spring.
I *have bitten* my nails since I was nine.

senses.head: Sting (of insects and snakes)
senses.body: In American usage mosquitoes, spiders, ants, and snakes *bite*; bees and wasps *sting*.
examples: Mosquitoes *bite* worst at dusk.
The mosquito *bit* me twice before I felt it.
She was *bitten* by a spider in the garage.

senses.head: Grip a surface, take hold
senses.body: Of tires, blades, screws, and anchors — anything that digs in rather than slipping.
examples: Winter tires *bite* into packed snow.
The blade *bit* deep into the log.
The anchor *had bitten* into the sand by then.

senses.head: Take effect painfully
senses.body: Of cold, wind, budget cuts, sanctions, or prices — the moment something stops being abstract and starts to hurt.
examples: The wind *bites* on that side of the building.
By then the cold *had bitten* through my gloves.
The new tariffs *bit* hardest in the smallest towns.

senses.head: Take the bait, respond to an offer
senses.body: Of fish, and figuratively of buyers or of anyone falling for a trick. Often negative: *nobody bit*.
examples: Trout *bite* best just after sunrise.
We advertised for a week and nobody *bit*.
Two buyers *have bitten* since we dropped the price.

senses.head: bite the bullet
senses.body: A fixed phrase: to accept something painful you have been putting off.
examples: You'll have to *bite* the bullet and tell her.
We finally *bit* the bullet and replaced the roof.
He *has bitten* the bullet on far worse repairs.

senses.head: bite your tongue, bite back
senses.body: To stop yourself from saying something. *Bite back* takes an object: *bite back a reply*.
examples: I *bit* my tongue and said nothing.
She had to *bite* back a laugh.
He *has bitten* his tongue through three straight meetings.

break.gloss: To separate something into pieces or stop it working — and, figuratively, to violate a rule, interrupt a state, or surpass a limit.

senses.head: Break into pieces, smash
senses.body: The literal core, transitive or intransitive. After *have* it is always *broken*: ✗ *I have broke it*.
examples: Glass jars *break* if you stack them.
He *broke* the vase reaching for the light.
Someone *had broken* the window before we arrived.

senses.head: Stop working, fail
senses.body: Of machines and devices. For cars and larger machinery Americans usually add *down*.
examples: Cheap chargers *break* within a month.
My phone *broke* the day the warranty ended.
The washing machine *has broken* twice this year.

senses.head: Fracture a bone
senses.body: Used of the person and of the bone alike: *he broke his wrist*, *his wrist broke*.
examples: Old bones *break* easily.
He *broke* his wrist on the ice last winter.
She *has broken* the same finger twice.

senses.head: Violate a rule, law, or promise
senses.body: Figurative but completely ordinary — *break the law*, *break a contract*, *break your word*.
examples: Don't *break* your promise to her.
The company *broke* the terms of the lease.
He *has broken* every rule in the handbook.

senses.head: Interrupt, put an end to a continuous state
senses.body: Of silence, a habit, a tie, a heat wave, a fall, a journey — anything that has been running unbroken.
examples: Nobody wanted to *break* the silence.
A branch *broke* his fall.
The rain *has broken* the heat wave at last.

senses.head: Beat a record or a limit
senses.body: Of records, thresholds, and numbers: *break a record*, *break four minutes*, *break a hundred degrees*.
examples: Records *break* at every Olympics.
She *broke* the state record in the 400.
Three runners *have broken* four minutes on this track.

senses.head: break the news, break a story
senses.body: To be the one who tells something for the first time — gently, in the case of bad news; first, in the case of journalism.
examples: She *breaks* the news gently whenever she can.
The paper *broke* the story on Sunday.
Someone *had broken* the news to him already.

senses.head: Of dawn, weather, or a voice
senses.body: A cluster of intransitive uses: day breaks, a storm breaks, and a voice breaks either with emotion or in adolescence.
examples: Day *breaks* around five in June.
His voice *broke* when he thanked her.
The storm *had broken* before we reached the car.

senses.head: break down
senses.ru: сломаться; сорваться, разрыдаться; разбить на части
senses.body: Three common uses: a vehicle or negotiation fails, a person loses composure, or something is separated into parts for analysis.
examples: *Break* the costs down by department.
Our car *broke* down on the interstate.
The talks *have broken* down completely.

senses.head: break up
senses.body: To end a relationship, to disperse a gathering, or to come apart into pieces. Of a phone call it means the signal is cutting out.
examples: Ice on the river *breaks* up in April.
They *broke* up after four years.
The meeting *had broken* up by noon.

senses.head: break in, break into
senses.body: *Break into* a building or a car is burglary; *break in* also means to soften new shoes or train a newcomer, and *break into* a market or a laugh starts something abruptly.
examples: It takes a week to *break* in new boots.
Someone *broke* into the garage last night.
Thieves *have broken* into three cars on this block.

senses.head: break out
senses.body: Of fires, wars, arguments, and epidemics starting suddenly; also of escaping from confinement, and of skin — *break out in a rash*.
examples: Fires *break* out in that canyon every August.
War *broke* out that September.
Two inmates *had broken* out through the laundry.

choose.gloss: To pick one thing out of several, or to decide on a course of action.

senses.head: Pick one out of several
senses.body: The core sense. Watch the spelling more than the tense: present *choose* /tʃuz/, past *chose* /tʃoʊz/, and there is no ✗ *choosed*.
examples: You *choose* the restaurant this time.
They *chose* the cheaper apartment.
We *have chosen* a name for the dog.

senses.head: choose to — decide to do something
senses.body: With an infinitive, meaning to do something deliberately rather than by default. Often used to underline that it was a free decision.
examples: People *choose* to live here for the quiet.
She *chose* to walk rather than wait for the bus.
He *has chosen* not to comment.

senses.head: Select someone for a role
senses.body: Of committees, voters, and teams. Very often passive: *she was chosen from a field of forty*.
examples: Each team *chooses* a captain in September.
Voters *chose* him by a wide margin.
The committee *had chosen* her before the interviews ended.

senses.head: choose between, choose from
senses.body: *Between* takes two options, *among* or *from* takes more. *There is nothing to choose between them* means they are equally good.
examples: You have to *choose* between the two offers.
She *chose* from a list of six.
I *have chosen* from this menu so often I know it by heart.

senses.head: chosen — selected, elect (adjective)
senses.body: As an adjective the participle carries a religious or elevated tone: *the chosen people*, *the chosen one*.
examples: He acts like the *chosen* one.
They saw themselves as a *chosen* people.

cleave.gloss: Two unrelated verbs share this spelling with nearly opposite meanings — to split something apart, and to cling to it. Both are regular in modern American English; *clove* and *cloven* survive only in fixed phrases and older writing.

senses.head: Split apart, chop in two
senses.body: The living form is *cleaved*; *clove* and *cloven* are archaic and will read as deliberate old-fashioned style.
examples: Frost can *cleave* a boulder in half.
One blow *clove* the log in two.
Lightning *had cloven* the old oak from crown to root.
Today a writer would simply say the axe *cleaved* the log.

senses.head: Cut through water or air
senses.body: Literary, of ships, blades, and aircraft moving cleanly through something.
examples: The jet *cleaves* the air with almost no noise.
The bow of the boat *clove* the water cleanly.
The prow *had cloven* a channel through the slush.

senses.head: cloven — split in two (adjective)
senses.body: Survives almost entirely in *cloven hoof* and *cloven foot*, and so carries a faint biblical or devilish echo.
examples: Goats and sheep have *cloven* hooves.
The devil is always drawn with a *cloven* foot.

senses.head: cleave to — cling, stay faithful to
senses.body: A separate verb that happens to be spelled the same; always regular (*cleaved to*), and formal or biblical in tone.
examples: She *cleaves* to the plan no matter what anyone says.
He *cleaved* to the old customs all his life.
They *have cleaved* to one another through worse than this.

delve.gloss: To dig — today almost always figuratively, into records, a subject, or the bottom of a bag. The strong forms *dolve* and *dolven* are archaic; modern usage is regular.

senses.head: delve into — research deeply
senses.body: By far the commonest use, and fully regular: *delve, delved, delved*. Almost always with *into*.
examples: Historians *delve* into letters and diaries for the real story.
She *delved* into the archive for three months.
Reporters *have delved* into his tax records.

senses.head: Dig in the ground
senses.body: The original literal sense, now archaic, and the one that carries the old forms *dolve* and *dolven* you will meet in older poetry and Bible translations.
examples: In older English the gardener *dolve* a trench along the wall.
Monks *had dolven* the well long before the abbey went up.
Miners *have delved* under these hills since the 1870s.

senses.head: Reach in and rummage
senses.body: Physical but small-scale: hunting through a bag, a drawer, or a pocket. Regular.
examples: She *delves* in her bag for a pen at every register.
He *delved* in his coat for the tickets.
I *have delved* through this drawer twice already.

forbear.gloss: To hold yourself back from doing something you could do — a formal verb, and the prefixed sibling of *bear*.

senses.head: Refrain from doing something
senses.body: Formal. Takes *from* + -ing, or, more literary still, a bare infinitive: *he forbore to answer*.
examples: Please *forbear* from calling before nine.
He *forbore* to mention the argument at dinner.
She *has forborne* every provocation for a month.

senses.head: Be patient, show restraint
senses.body: Without an object: to put up with something instead of reacting. The noun *forbearance* is more common than the verb.
examples: A good editor *forbears* where a proud one would argue.
The neighbors *forbore* for years before they complained.
We *have forborne* long enough.

senses.head: Hold off on collecting a debt
senses.body: A banking term: a lender pauses payments instead of declaring default. You will meet it as the noun *forbearance* on loan paperwork.
examples: Lenders may *forbear* for up to twelve months.
The servicer *forbore* while she was out of work.
The bank *had forborne* on the loan for two quarters.

forget.gloss: To fail to remember something — a fact, an intention, an object left behind — or to deliberately put it out of your mind.

senses.head: Fail to remember
senses.body: The core sense. In American English the participle is *forgotten* without exception: ✗ *I have forgot his name*.
examples: I always *forget* where I parked.
She *forgot* his name halfway through the introduction.
She *has forgotten* more about engines than I ever knew.

senses.head: Fail to do something you meant to
senses.body: With an infinitive. Compare *forget doing*, which means failing to remember an event that already happened — a different thing entirely.
examples: Don't *forget* to lock the back door.
He *forgot* to set the alarm.
We *had forgotten* to book a table.

senses.head: Leave something behind
senses.body: Ordinary in speech, though careful writers use *leave* once the place is named: *I left my passport at the hotel*.
examples: Try not to *forget* your badge again.
He *forgot* his passport at the hotel.
I *have forgotten* my umbrella in three cabs this year.

senses.head: Put out of your mind, stop dwelling on
senses.body: Deliberate rather than accidental, usually with *about*. This is the sense in *forgive and forget*.
examples: *Forget* about work for one weekend.
She never *forgot* what he said that night.
We *had forgotten* how loud the city gets in summer.

senses.head: forget it
senses.ru: забудь; не стоит благодарности; ни за что
senses.body: A frozen imperative that means 'never mind', 'don't mention it', or a flat refusal, depending entirely on tone.
examples: *Forget* it — it wasn't important.
'Can I borrow the truck?' '*Forget* it.'

senses.head: forget yourself
senses.body: Reflexive and somewhat dated: to behave improperly because you lost your composure.
examples: He *forgot* himself and raised his voice at the front desk.
She *had* never *forgotten* herself in public before.

forswear.gloss: To give something up formally, or to renounce it under oath — the prefixed sibling of *swear*.

senses.head: Renounce, give up formally
senses.body: Formal, and stronger than *give up*: it implies a public or binding commitment.
examples: The monks here *forswear* private property.
He *forswore* sugar in January and lasted nine days.
She *has forsworn* social media entirely.

senses.head: Swear never to do something again
senses.body: With a noun or an -ing form. Close to *swear off*, which is the everyday American phrasing.
examples: I *forswear* nothing until I've slept on it.
After the audit they *forswore* cash payments altogether.
He *had forsworn* gambling twice before.

senses.head: forswear yourself — perjure yourself
senses.body: Reflexive and legal: to lie under oath. A *forsworn* witness is a perjurer, not someone who has renounced something.
examples: A man who *forswears* himself in court risks prison.
The witness *had forsworn* himself twice before the trial ended.

freeze.gloss: To turn to ice or be gripped by cold — and figuratively to stop dead, to stop responding, or to hold money and prices where they are.

senses.head: Turn to ice, become frozen
senses.body: The literal sense, intransitive. After *have* it is always *frozen*: ✗ *the pipes have froze*.
examples: Lakes up north *freeze* by early December.
The pond *froze* solid overnight.
The ground *had frozen* before they could dig.

senses.head: Be painfully cold (of a person)
senses.body: Hyperbolic and usually progressive — *I'm freezing* — or in *freeze to death*, which almost never means literally dying.
examples: You'll *freeze* out there without a hat.
We *froze* on the sidelines for two hours.
I *have frozen* at every one of his games this season.

senses.head: Preserve food by freezing
senses.body: Transitive and everyday. The participle doubles as the familiar adjective: *frozen peas*, *frozen dinner*.
examples: *Freeze* the extra soup in small containers.
She *froze* six quarts of berries in August.
We *have frozen* half the batch already.

senses.head: Stop moving suddenly
senses.body: Of a person or animal stopped by fear or surprise. The police command *Freeze!* comes from here.
examples: Deer *freeze* in headlights.
She *froze* when she heard footsteps behind her.
He *had frozen* halfway down the ladder.

senses.head: Of a screen or program: stop responding
senses.body: The standard computing use, intransitive, and the one learners meet daily.
examples: The app *freezes* whenever I open a large file.
The video *froze* right at the punchline.
My laptop *has frozen* three times today.

senses.head: Hold prices, wages, or hiring in place
senses.body: Transitive, from business and government. The matching noun is *a freeze*: *a hiring freeze*.
examples: The board voted to *freeze* tuition for a year.
The company *froze* hiring in March.
The state *has frozen* utility rates twice since 2020.

senses.head: Block access to money or assets
senses.body: A legal and banking use: a court, a bank, or a regulator makes funds untouchable.
examples: A judge can *freeze* an account within hours.
The bank *froze* the card after two odd charges.
Regulators *have frozen* the firm's assets.

senses.head: freeze out — exclude
senses.body: To shut someone out of a group, a deal, or a market by treating them as though they were not there.
examples: They *freeze* out anyone who asks questions.
The partners *froze* him out of the decision.
Small vendors *have been frozen* out of the market.

senses.head: freeze up — lock up, be unable to act
senses.body: Of a person going blank under pressure, and of a mechanism seizing.
examples: Some people *freeze* up on camera.
He *froze* up during the interview.
I *have frozen* up in front of an audience more than once.

hide.gloss: To put something where it cannot be found, to go where you cannot be seen, or to keep something secret.

senses.head: Put something out of sight
senses.body: Transitive and literal. The participle is *hidden*: ✗ *he has hid the key*.
examples: We *hide* the gifts in the attic every year.
He *hid* the spare key under a flowerpot.
Someone *has hidden* the remote again.

senses.head: Conceal yourself
senses.body: Intransitive, of people and animals getting out of view.
examples: Kids *hide* behind the couch during thunderstorms.
She *hid* in the stairwell until they left.
The cat *had hidden* under the porch all afternoon.

senses.head: Keep secret, conceal facts or feelings
senses.body: Figurative and very common: information, a diagnosis, an emotion, a number in a footnote.
examples: She doesn't *hide* her opinions.
The report *hid* the real numbers in a footnote.
He *has hidden* the diagnosis from his family for months.

senses.head: Cover from view
senses.body: Of a thing that blocks sight of something else — clouds, a hedge, snow — with no intention involved.
examples: Clouds *hide* the summit most mornings.
A hedge *hid* the house from the road.
The path *had been hidden* by new snow.

senses.head: hide out, go into hiding
senses.body: To stay concealed somewhere for a stretch of time, usually from the police, the press, or an obligation.
examples: Suspects usually *hide* out with relatives.
He *hid* out in a motel for a week.
They *have hidden* out in the mountains since the indictment.

interweave.gloss: To weave two or more things together — threads literally, stories, lives, or themes figuratively.

senses.head: Weave strands together
senses.body: The literal textile sense, transitive. Unlike plain *weave*, it has no regular alternative: ✗ *interweaved*.
examples: Weavers here *interweave* wool and linen in the same cloth.
The artist *interwove* copper wire and silk thread.
Craftsmen *have interwoven* the two fibers for centuries.

senses.head: Work several elements into a whole
senses.body: Where the verb actually lives in modern writing — of plots, melodies, arguments, and families.
examples: Good novels *interweave* several lives without losing any of them.
The score *interweaves* three folk melodies.
Their families *had interwoven* through four generations of marriages.
The two plots *have interwoven* so tightly you cannot follow one alone.

senses.head: interwoven — closely connected (adjective)
senses.body: The participle does most of this verb's work in real American prose: *interwoven storylines*, *interwoven fates*.
examples: Politics and money are thoroughly *interwoven* here.
The two economies are deeply *interwoven*.

misspeak.gloss: To say the wrong thing by mistake — in American public life, the standard way to take a statement back without calling it a lie.

senses.head: Misstate something, say the wrong thing
senses.body: Nearly always about oneself and nearly always in the past: *I misspoke* concedes an error while denying intent.
examples: If I *misspeak*, please correct me.
The senator *misspoke* about the date of the vote.
He admits he *has misspoken* twice this week.

senses.head: Say or pronounce badly
senses.body: The older, plainer sense — getting a word, a name, or a line out wrong. Rarer than the political use above.
examples: Even careful people *misspeak* when they are tired.
The announcer *misspoke* the winner's name on live television.
She realized she *had misspoken* the moment the words left her mouth.

speak.gloss: To use the voice to say words — to talk, to hold a conversation, to use a language, or to address an audience.

senses.head: Say words, talk
senses.body: The bare sense, usually with an adverb or in the negative. This is the model verb for the whole group: ✗ *I have spoke*.
examples: Please *speak* more slowly.
He *spoke* very quietly.
Nobody *had spoken* for a full minute.

senses.head: speak to, speak with — talk to someone
senses.body: *Speak to* and *speak with* are both American; *with* sounds a shade more mutual, *to* a shade more one-directional.
examples: *Speak* with your advisor before you drop the class.
I *spoke* to the landlord yesterday.
She *has spoken* with all three references.

senses.head: Know and use a language
senses.body: Transitive, with a language as the object, and never progressive in this sense: ✗ *I am speaking Spanish* to mean you know it.
examples: We *speak* Spanish at home.
She *spoke* almost no English when she arrived.
I *have spoken* Russian since childhood.

senses.head: Give a talk, address an audience
senses.body: Intransitive, usually with *at*, *to*, or *on*. The related noun is *speaker*.
examples: The dean *speaks* at every graduation.
He *spoke* for twenty minutes without notes.
She *has spoken* at three conferences this year.

senses.head: speak up
senses.body: Two everyday uses: talk louder so you can be heard, and volunteer an opinion or an offer in a group.
examples: *Speak* up, please — we can't hear you in back.
Nobody *spoke* up when he asked for volunteers.
One student *has spoken* up at every meeting.

senses.head: speak out
senses.body: Stronger than *speak up*: to state a public objection, usually at some risk. Often *speak out against*.
examples: Few employees *speak* out in meetings like that.
Teachers *spoke* out against the new schedule.
Several officers *have spoken* out since the report.

senses.head: speak your mind
senses.body: A fixed phrase for saying exactly what you think, with the implication that most people would not.
examples: She *speaks* her mind at every meeting.
He *spoke* his mind and lost the account.
I *have spoken* my mind often enough here.

senses.head: speak for — represent; vouch for
senses.body: To act as someone's voice, or to attest to their quality. *Speak for yourself* is a mild rebuke.
examples: I *speak* for the whole department here.
She *spoke* for the family at the hearing.
He *has spoken* for that community for twenty years.

senses.head: speak for itself, speak volumes
senses.ru: говорить само за себя, быть красноречивым
senses.body: Fixed phrases with a thing as the subject: the evidence needs no comment.
examples: The numbers *speak* for themselves.
Her silence *spoke* volumes.
The results *have spoken* for themselves all season.

senses.head: so to speak, generally speaking
senses.body: Frozen phrases used as sentence adverbs — hedging a metaphor, framing a generalization, or changing the subject with *speaking of*.
examples: He's the mayor of this block, *so to speak*.
*Speaking* of rent, mine went up again.

steal.gloss: To take what is not yours — and by extension to move quietly, to snatch a small pleasure, or to take the attention away from someone else.

senses.head: Take without permission
senses.body: The core sense. You *steal* the thing and *rob* the person or place: ✗ *they stole the bank*. The passive is where the participle error shows up: ✗ *my bike has been stole*.
examples: Raccoons *steal* food right off the grill.
Someone *stole* my umbrella from the lobby.
Two paintings *have been stolen* from the museum.
He learned his car *had been stolen* only that morning.

senses.head: Take an idea or work as your own
senses.body: Of plagiarism, borrowed jokes, and copied designs — no physical object changes hands.
examples: Big labels *steal* from small ones all the time.
He *stole* the line from an old movie.
She claims they *have stolen* her design.

senses.head: Take quickly and quietly
senses.body: Of a glance, a kiss, a nap, an hour — something small taken when nobody is looking or when there is no time for it.
examples: I *steal* twenty minutes with a book after lunch.
He *stole* a look at his phone under the table.
We *have stolen* whole afternoons this way.

senses.head: Move quietly, sneak
senses.body: Intransitive and literary, usually with a direction: *steal away*, *steal into*, *steal out*.
examples: Fog *steals* up the valley every evening.
She *stole* out of the house before dawn.
He *had stolen* back to his seat unnoticed.

senses.head: steal the show, steal the scene
senses.body: To attract all the attention at an event, usually without meaning to and usually from a smaller role.
examples: She *steals* every scene she is in.
The dog *stole* the show at the wedding.
That trumpet solo *has stolen* the whole record.

senses.head: steal someone's thunder
senses.body: To take the credit or the moment someone else had prepared, typically by getting there first.
examples: Don't let the opening act *steal* your thunder.
He *stole* her thunder by announcing it first.
The leak *had stolen* the mayor's thunder completely.

senses.head: steal a base (baseball)
senses.body: To advance a base while the pitch is being thrown, without a hit. A standard American sports use with its own statistic, *stolen bases*.
examples: Fast runners *steal* bases in close games.
He *stole* second on the first pitch.
She *has stolen* thirty bases this season.

swear.gloss: To make a solemn promise or take an oath — and, in the everyday sense, to use profanity.

senses.head: Use profanity
senses.body: Intransitive, with *at* someone or *about* something. The commonest sense in speech; *curse* is the more formal synonym.
examples: My uncle *swears* every time his team loses.
He *swore* at the referee and got thrown out.
She *has* never *sworn* in front of the kids.

senses.head: Make a solemn promise or oath
senses.body: The formal sense, with *to* + verb or with a noun object: *swear an oath*, *swear allegiance*. The participle is *sworn*: ✗ *I have swore*.
examples: Witnesses *swear* to tell the truth.
They *swore* an oath of loyalty.
He *has sworn* to finish what she started.

senses.head: Insist emphatically
senses.body: *I swear* plus a clause — a way of pressing a claim when you expect not to be believed. Informal.
examples: I *swear* I locked the door.
She *swore* she had mailed the check.
He *has sworn* up and down that he never saw the email.

senses.head: swear someone in
senses.body: Of officials, juries, and witnesses taking office or the stand. Usually passive: *the jury was sworn in*.
examples: They *swear* in the new council on Monday.
The chief justice *swore* him in on the Capitol steps.
The jury *had been sworn* in before lunch.

senses.head: swear off
senses.body: To give up a habit deliberately and announce it — coffee, cable, late nights.
examples: People *swear* off sugar every January.
She *swore* off cable and never looked back.
He *has sworn* off coffee after six o'clock.

senses.head: swear by
senses.ru: полностью доверять, души не чаять в
senses.body: To have complete faith in a remedy, a brand, or a method. Not to be confused with *swear at*, which is the profanity sense.
examples: My mother *swears* by this cough syrup.
He *swore* by that mechanic for thirty years.
Runners *have sworn* by these shoes for a decade.

tear.gloss: To pull something apart by force — and, of a person or vehicle, to move very fast. The verb *tear* /tɛr/ rhymes with *air*; the noun *tear* /tɪr/ that means a drop from the eye is a different word.

senses.head: Rip, pull apart
senses.body: The core transitive sense. After *have* it is *torn*: ✗ *I have tore it*.
examples: Please don't *tear* the wrapping paper.
He *tore* the letter into four pieces.
The storm *had torn* the awning loose.

senses.head: Come apart, get ripped
senses.body: The intransitive half of the same idea, with the fabric or paper as the subject.
examples: Thin paper *tears* if you pull it flat.
The seam *tore* the first time he wore it.
My jacket *has torn* at the elbow.

senses.head: Wrench away, pull off by force
senses.body: With *from*, *out of*, or *off*. Also reflexive — *tear yourself away* from something absorbing.
examples: Storms like that *tear* shingles right off the roof.
She *tore* the page out of the notebook.
He *has torn* himself away from that screen exactly once today.

senses.head: Injure a muscle or ligament
senses.body: Standard sports-medicine use; the matching noun is *a tear* /tɛr/ — *an ACL tear*.
examples: Runners *tear* muscles when they skip the warm-up.
He *tore* a ligament in the second half.
She *has torn* the same hamstring twice.

senses.head: be torn between — passive
senses.body: Passive only, of a person or a group pulled two ways by loyalties or options.
examples: The town was *torn* between two proposals.
I am *torn* between the two offers.
She *had been torn* about it for weeks.

senses.head: Move very fast
senses.body: Informal and intransitive, always with a direction: *tear down the street*, *tear out of the lot*, *tear around*.
examples: Kids *tear* around the yard until dark.
He *tore* out of the driveway without looking.
The truck *had torn* past us on the shoulder.

senses.head: tear down, tear up, tear apart
senses.ru: сносить; разорвать в клочья; разнести, расколоть
senses.body: *Tear down* is to demolish a building or discredit a person; *tear up* is to rip to shreds (and, from the noun, to start crying, /tɪr/); *tear apart* is to destroy or divide.
examples: Developers *tear* down houses like that every week.
She *tore* up the contract in front of him.
The scandal *has torn* the party apart.

unfreeze.gloss: To release something from a frozen state — ice, money, prices, or a stuck screen.

senses.head: Thaw, release from ice
senses.body: The literal sense. For food Americans normally say *thaw* or *defrost*; *unfreeze* survives mainly for pipes, locks, and ground.
examples: Run warm water over the joint to *unfreeze* the pipe.
Warm rain *unfroze* the top layer of soil.
The line *has unfrozen* on its own.

senses.head: Release blocked funds or assets
senses.body: The commonest use in the news, usually of a court, a bank, or a government reversing a freeze.
examples: Sanctions relief would *unfreeze* billions.
The court *unfroze* the family's bank accounts in April.
Congress *has unfrozen* the aid package.

senses.head: Lift a freeze on prices, wages, or hiring
senses.body: The administrative counterpart of *freeze*: budgets, salaries, tuition, and rents go back to moving.
examples: The board voted to *unfreeze* salaries in July.
The agency *unfroze* rates after the lawsuit.
The hiring budget *had been unfrozen* weeks before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Get a stuck screen or program going again
senses.body: Everyday computing use, transitive. Note that the finite past *unfroze* sounds odd to many readers here; *got it unfrozen* is commoner in speech.
examples: A restart usually *unfreezes* the screen.
Nothing *unfroze* the app but a full reboot.
The update *has unfrozen* the interface for most users.

wake.gloss: To stop sleeping, or to rouse someone from sleep — in everyday American speech almost always with *up*.

senses.head: Stop sleeping
senses.body: Intransitive. American edited prose wants *woken* after *have*; British English tolerates *have woke*, and the regular *waked* is also allowed but sounds dated.
examples: I *wake* at six without an alarm.
She *woke* twice in the night.
He *has woken* at odd hours ever since the trip.

senses.head: Rouse someone from sleep
senses.body: Transitive. Keep it clear of the slang adjective *woke*, which is unrelated to the verb's tenses.
examples: Try not to *wake* anyone on your way out.
The thunder *woke* the baby.
The dog *had woken* us before the alarm went off.

senses.head: wake up
senses.body: The ordinary spoken form, both intransitive and transitive. As an imperative it also means 'pay attention, face facts'.
examples: *Wake* up — we're here.
He *woke* up on the couch again.
She *has woken* up early all week.

senses.head: wake up to — become aware of
senses.body: To finally register a problem that has been there all along.
examples: We *wake* up to these things too late.
The industry finally *woke* up to the problem.
Voters *have woken* up to what it costs.

senses.head: Stir up, rouse (feelings, memories)
senses.body: Figurative and transitive; the more literary [awake](#awake) covers the same ground.
examples: Old letters *wake* feelings you thought were done with.
The song *woke* something in her.
The election *had woken* a part of the state nobody had polled.

wear.gloss: To have clothing or an accessory on your body — and, in a second family of senses, to reduce or damage something gradually through use.

senses.head: Have clothing on
senses.body: The core sense, and one of the highest-frequency verbs in the language. After *have* it is *worn*: ✗ *she has wore that coat*.
examples: Most people here *wear* boots all winter.
He *wore* the same tie to every interview.
She *has worn* those earrings every day this month.

senses.head: Have a hairstyle, expression, or look
senses.body: Extends past clothes to anything you carry on your person or your face: a beard, a smile, a look of confusion, cologne.
examples: She *wears* her hair short now.
He *wore* a look of complete confusion.
He *has worn* a beard since college.

senses.head: Damage or reduce through use
senses.body: Transitive, of friction over time: *wear a hole*, *wear a groove*, *wear something smooth*.
examples: Traffic *wears* the paint off the crosswalk every year.
Water *wore* a channel through the rock.
The stairs *had worn* smooth in the middle.

senses.head: Become thin or damaged with use
senses.body: The intransitive half. *Wear well* is a compliment — it means something (or someone) ages without deteriorating.
examples: Cheap fabric *wears* badly.
The soles *wore* out in a single season.
The rug *has worn* through by the door.

senses.head: wear out
senses.body: Of an object used until it is useless, and of a person exhausted by something. Also *wear out your welcome*.
examples: Those kids *wear* me out.
He *wore* out three pairs of shoes on the trail.
I *have worn* myself out arguing about this.

senses.head: wear off
senses.body: Of an effect fading: medication, novelty, shock, the numbness after the dentist.
examples: Wait until the numbness *wears* off.
The novelty *wore* off in a week.
The excitement *has worn* off completely.

senses.head: wear down
senses.body: To weaken someone's resistance by persistence rather than force; also literal, of surfaces ground away.
examples: Constant delays *wear* down even patient clients.
They *wore* him down with phone calls.
The campaign *had worn* her down by October.

senses.head: wear on
senses.body: Two uses: of time passing slowly — *as the evening wore on* — and of something grating on a person.
examples: His whistling *wears* on me.
As the afternoon *wore* on, fewer people stayed.
The wait *has worn* on everyone.

senses.head: worn — shabby, tired (adjective)
senses.body: The participle stands alone as an adjective, of objects and of faces — a useful reminder that *worn*, not *wore*, is the form that follows *have* and *be*.
examples: He came in with a *worn* jacket and a *worn* face.
The book is *worn* at the spine.

weave.gloss: To make cloth or baskets by crossing strands — and, figuratively, to work several elements into one whole. Winding through traffic is the regular *weaved*.

senses.head: Make cloth on a loom
senses.body: The literal textile sense, and the one that firmly takes *wove/woven*.
examples: They *weave* rugs on a loom older than the house.
Her grandmother *wove* blankets for the whole family.
Villagers here *have woven* silk for six generations.
The scarf is *woven* from two kinds of wool.

senses.head: Make by interlacing strands
senses.body: Baskets, wreaths, fences, hair — anything built by crossing flexible material.
examples: Children *weave* wreaths out of clover.
She *wove* a basket out of river reeds.
He *had woven* a fence out of willow branches.

senses.head: Work several elements into a whole
senses.body: Figurative, of stories, arguments, music, and lectures. Usually *weave something into something*.
examples: He *weaves* jokes into serious lectures.
The author *had woven* the letters into the narrative.
She *has woven* three timelines into one story.

senses.head: Move winding through
senses.body: This sense is regular — *weaved, weaved*: ✓ *the cab weaved across three lanes*, ✗ *the cab wove across three lanes*.
examples: Cyclists *weave* through stopped traffic all day.
The runner *weaved* through the pack on the last lap.
He *has weaved* in and out of that lane for a mile.
